q: Most of the region's planted area belongs to whom?
opts: The cooperatives, which own it outright
exp: The average holding is measured in a few hectares and sometimes in fractions of one. That imbalance is why supply contracts and cooperative membership shape the entire trade.

q: The majority of Champagne carries no year on the label. What is that blend meant to achieve?
opts: A wine from a single vineyard
The shortest possible time before sale
exp: The climate is marginal enough that any single harvest can disappoint. Blending across years, villages and varieties is how a house repeats one recognisable style from one year to the next, and how it makes a difficult vintage taste like a fine one.

q: Older wines held back in tank or cask are worked into each new blend. What are they called?
exp: Some houses keep a perpetual reserve, topped up at every harvest and drawn from continuously, so a trace of many past vintages runs through every bottle they sell.

q: When a house declares a vintage, what must be true of the wine?
opts: At least eighty-five percent comes from that harvest
All of it comes from that single harvest
It contains no reserve wine older than five years
exp: Declaration is a judgement rather than an entitlement. A house declares only when it believes the year merits it, and in a poor run it may skip several years together.

q: Created for a Russian tsar and still sold in clear glass, Cristal belongs to which house?
exp: The clear bottle was reputedly made so that nothing could be concealed inside it. A prestige cuvee is a house's flagship, drawn from its best crus and given the longest ageing.

q: Comtes de Champagne, a Blanc de Blancs, is the prestige cuvee of which house?
exp: It is named for the counts who ruled the region in the Middle Ages, and it is drawn from Grand Cru Chardonnay on the Cote des Blancs.

q: Not every prestige cuvee carries a year. Which is the best-known example that does not?
exp: Grande Cuvee is a multi-vintage blend of well over a hundred separate wines and is the house's signature bottling, though its single-vineyard cuvees sit above it. A vintage date is not what defines the tier.

q: Before release, a non-vintage wine must rest on its lees in bottle for a minimum period. How long?
exp: Fifteen months must pass in total between tirage and sale, of which at least twelve are on the lees. Serious houses treat those figures as a floor and routinely double them.

q: A vintage wine faces a longer legal minimum. What is it?
exp: Three years is the floor, and many houses hold vintage wines far longer before disgorging. That extra time builds the toasted, nutty register the category is bought for.

q: Bollinger's R.D. stands for recemment degorge. What does the label promise?
opts: Fermentation in stainless steel rather than in oak
No dosage of any kind at disgorgement
A single vineyard as the source of the fruit
Long lees ageing, then recent disgorgement
exp: Recently disgorged. The wine keeps the protection of lees contact for years longer, then reaches the table with the vigour of a young disgorgement and the depth of an old wine.

q: Many producers now print the disgorgement date on the back label. What does it let a buyer judge?
opts: The dosage the wine received in grams per litre
How long the wine has been off its lees
exp: A wine changes faster once the lees are gone and oxygen begins to reach it past the cork. Two bottles of one cuvee disgorged years apart can taste markedly different.

q: What does an unusually long stay on the lees do to the bubble itself?
opts: It makes the bubbles noticeably coarser
It makes the mousse finer and more persistent
exp: Mannoproteins released by the dying yeast lower surface tension and hold carbon dioxide more tightly. The result is a creamy bead rather than a coarse froth.

q: At what temperature is a young non-vintage best poured?
exp: Cold enough to keep the mousse lively, warm enough for the aroma to show at all. Serving near freezing mutes the fruit and hardens the acidity.

q: A mature prestige cuvee is often served a few degrees warmer than a young Brut. Why?
opts: Its complex aromatics need the warmth to open
Warmth raises the pressure in the bottle
Cold would strip out the dosage
exp: Ten to twelve degrees suits an old vintage wine. Treat it much as you would a fine white Burgundy rather than as an aperitif fizz.

q: Opening a bottle safely begins with a thumb held over the cork. How far is the wire cage then loosened?
opts: It is lifted off entirely before anything else
Six half-turns of the wire loop
exp: Six half-turns frees the cage on every muselet made. The thumb stays put throughout, because a cork under six atmospheres travels faster than anyone can react.

q: With the cage loosened, which part should be turned?
opts: Neither, the cork is levered upward
The bottle, while the cork is held still
The cork, while the bottle is held still
exp: Turning the base gives control and eases the cork out with a sigh rather than a report. Holding the bottle at about forty-five degrees reduces the chance of it foaming over.
